topic: Geography means 'Earth-writing'; the word was first used by Eratosthenes, who also measured the Earth's circumference.
Ancient Babylonians, Greeks, Chinese and Indians mapped and described their known worlds; Ptolemy's 'Geography' set the method for 1,400 years.
Islamic and Chinese geographers advanced mapmaking in the Middle Ages; the European voyages of exploration remade the world map from the 15th century.
Geography became a university discipline in the 19th century (Humboldt, Ritter); since then it has moved through regional, quantitative and critical schools, and GIS.

Egypt: Egyptians saw the Nile as the centre of the world.
They knew oases to the east and west, Kush to the south and Punt along the Red Sea.
Neighbouring peoples were named Retenu, Canaan and the Hittites (Khatti).
Babylon: The oldest known world maps come from Babylon.
The Babylonian Map of the World (about 600 BC) shows Babylon at the centre of a circular land surrounded by a 'bitter river' (ocean).
Seven islands beyond the ocean form a seven-pointed star.
Greco-Roman world: Greeks saw Homer as the first geographer; Anaximander drew the first Greek world map.
Herodotus described the peoples and lands of the known world; Aristotle argued that the Earth is a sphere.
Eratosthenes measured the Earth's circumference and coined the word 'geography'; Strabo wrote a 17-volume 'Geography'.
Ptolemy's 'Geography' (2nd century) listed places by latitude and longitude, a method used until the Renaissance.
India: The Vedas and Puranas describe rivers, mountains and the regions of India.
Indian geography was interwoven with Hindu mythology and pilgrimage.
The 'Arthashastra' and astronomers such as Aryabhata dealt with territory and the Earth's size.
China: The 'Yu Gong' (5th century BC) describes China's nine provinces, their soils and products.
Zhang Qian's travels opened routes to Central Asia; Pei Xiu (3rd century) set out principles of mapmaking with a grid scale.
The 'Commentary on the Water Classic' described China's rivers; Shen Kuo made relief maps and described the magnetic compass.
Middle Ages: Byzantine scholars such as Stephanus of Byzantium compiled geographical dictionaries.
Islamic geographers such as al-Khwarizmi, Ibn Khordadbeh, al-Balkhi and Ibn Hawqal mapped and described the Muslim world.
Al-Idrisi's world map (1154) for Roger II of Sicily was one of the most accurate of its time.
In Europe, T-and-O maps showed a religious world view; travellers such as Marco Polo widened knowledge of Asia.
Early modern period: Ptolemy's 'Geography' was rediscovered in Europe around 1400.
Voyages of discovery (Columbus, da Gama, Magellan) remade the world map; Waldseemüller's map (1507) first named 'America'.
Mercator's projection (1569) made navigation easier; Kant lectured on physical geography.
19th century: Geography became a university discipline, especially in Germany and France.
Alexander von Humboldt and Carl Ritter founded modern geography; Humboldt linked climate, plants and landscape.
Geographical societies sponsored exploration of Africa, the Arctic and Antarctica.
20th century: Geography passed through four main approaches: environmental determinism, regional geography, the quantitative revolution and critical geography.
Halford Mackinder's 'heartland' theory (1904) linked geography to world power.
The quantitative revolution of the 1950s–60s brought statistics and models; Tobler's 'first law' says near things are more related than distant ones.
Critical geographers from the 1970s studied power, inequality and society.
21st century: Geographic information systems (GIS) and satellite data dominate much of the field.
Quantitative and critical geographers have moved from conflict to coexistence.
Human–environment questions, such as climate change, are central.
